analysis.one_liner: Delays union elections by weeks and makes it harder to strike employer workplace rules.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote in the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite National Labor Relations Board rules for union elections. It would require the board to wait at least 14 days before holding the pre-election hearing and at least 20 business days after ordering an election before actually holding it, and to resolve every hearing challenge before certifying results. It would force the board to consider folding more workers into a bargaining unit unless they are 'sufficiently distinct,' undoing the current practice of allowing smaller units. It would also make it much harder to find that an employer's workplace rule violates labor law, requiring clear and convincing evidence that harm to workers outweighs the employer's justification.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing drives gain the most. Every waiting period extends the window between a petition and a vote, giving management more time to campaign against the union while workers wait. The bargaining-unit provisions push toward larger, harder-to-organize units, and the handbook provision protects employer work rules from legal challenge unless an employee can meet a clear-and-convincing evidence standard.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the board from holding a pre-election hearing until at least 14 days after a union petition is filed and from holding the election until at least 20 business days after it is directed, slowing every unionization campaign [S2][S3].
Requires the board to rule on all hearing issues and challenges before certifying an election, adding more delay and opportunity for litigation [S2][S3].

Requires the board to apply a 'sufficient community of interest' analysis and forbids excluding workers from a unit unless their interests are sufficiently distinct, pushing unions toward broader, harder-to-win units [S2][S3].

Makes facially neutral employer rules, policies, and handbook provisions presumptively lawful unless the NLRB General Counsel shows by clear and convincing evidence that harm to workers' rights outweighs the employer's justification [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to form or join a union. They would wait longer before voting, could be swept into larger units where organizing a majority is harder, and would face a much higher evidentiary bar to overturn employer rules used against them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers trying to organize a union

drawbacks.text: Supporters argue quick elections deny employers adequate time to respond, and that the board's practice of deferring some issues until after the vote leaves unresolved questions that fuel litigation; the bill's mandatory timeline and requirement to decide all challenges before certification are the stated fix [S3].

The costs are borne by workers: lengthened election timelines are widely recognized to give employers more time to campaign against organizing and to take adverse actions against union supporters before the vote, and the handbook provision raises the evidentiary standard for challenging employer rules to 'clear and convincing evidence' [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to employers and its costs to workers' organizing rights; nothing in the text offers workers a compensating gain. The delays it mandates are precisely the period in which employers have the greatest ability to influence the outcome, so the design stacks the timeline in one side's favor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Walberg introduced the bill on June 5, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S1][S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill, and the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4][S5].
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers' current organizing rights remain unchanged: nothing about union elections, bargaining units, or employer rules has been altered because the bill never moved. Employers who would have gained longer timelines and rule protections gained nothing, and the National Labor Relations Board's existing procedures stand.

for.name: Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; no other member of either party cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a single cosponsor from either party and never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the parties would have lined up; its lone sponsor was a Republican running on a platform of rolling back what the bill calls the 'ambush election rule' [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would give these employers weeks of extra time between a union petition and a vote, larger default bargaining units, and a clear-and-convincing evidence standard before their workplace rules can be struck down. Each provision shifts leverage during organizing drives toward management and away from workers.

Mandatory waiting periods, broader required bargaining units, and delayed certification would slow campaigns and make winning a majority harder. Unions and their members' interest here runs with workers' own interest.
